topic: Prepositional Phrases, Time, Place, Direction, Context Shifts & Usage Traps

situationBrief.title: Prepositions
situationBrief.description: Learn how prepositions bridge nouns to sentences across time, place, direction, and means—and why context shapes every choice.

grammarOutcomes: Identify Prepositions and complete Prepositional Phrases (Preposition + Noun / Noun Group / Object Pronoun) and see how swapping a preposition changes meaning.
Select accurate prepositions of Time (at, on, in, since, for, during, by, until), Static Place (at, in, on, between, among, beside), and Direction (into, onto, to, towards, across, through, along).
Interpret context-dependent prepositions (by, with, in, of/from), avoid extra prepositions after transitive verbs (discuss, enter, reach), and separate prepositions from phrasal verbs.
learningObjectives.knowledgeOutcome: Explore Indian school gardens, courtyard maps, Godavari train journeys, and healthy kitchen scenes through interactive prepositional bridges.

sentences.title: Starter Sentence · Relation Bridge ('on')
sentences.rawText: The brass bottle sits on the wooden bench.
sentences.note: The preposition 'on' links 'the wooden bench' to 'sits', showing the bottle touches the top surface.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Tells what the bottle is made of.
Names what the sentence is about.

tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Connects 'the wooden bench' to 'sits'. Swapping 'on' for 'under' or 'beside' changes the scene!
Part of the Preposition's Object noun group.
Part of the Object noun group 'the wooden bench'.
Head-noun of the Prepositional Phrase 'on the wooden bench'.

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'The brass bottle' is the Subject.
groups.textbookRule: Subjects name who or what the sentence is about.

groups.label: Predicate (Verb + Prepositional Phrase)
groups.plainExplanation: 'sits' + Prepositional Phrase 'on the wooden bench' (Preposition 'on' + Object 'the wooden bench').
groups.textbookRule: A preposition joins a noun or noun group to show a spatial, time, or logical relation.

structureSummary.patternNote: Bridge: sits (Verb) <- on (Preposition) -> the wooden bench (Object).

sentences.title: Compare Sentence · Meaning Shift ('under')
sentences.rawText: The brass bottle sits under the wooden bench.
sentences.note: Changing one word—'on' -> 'under'—moves the bottle from the top of the bench to the ground beneath it!

tokens.meaningInSentence: Moves the bottle below the bench.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Swapping the preposition shifts the spatial relationship completely.

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'The brass bottle' (unchanged).
groups.textbookRule: Prepositions control the relationship between unchanged nouns.

groups.label: Predicate
groups.plainExplanation: 'under' replaced 'on', placing the bottle underneath instead of on top.
groups.textbookRule: Swapping a preposition alters meaning directly.

sentences.title: Starter Sentence · Full Prepositional Phrase
sentences.rawText: Fresh spinach grows near the water tank.
sentences.note: A Prepositional Phrase includes the preposition ('near') PLUS its entire noun group ('the water tank')—never split off 'the' or 'water'!

tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Starts the Prepositional Phrase 'near the water tank' (no finite verb inside!).

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'Fresh spinach' is the Subject.
groups.textbookRule: Prepositional phrases inside a Subject or Predicate keep their full noun group together.

groups.label: Predicate
groups.questionPrompt: What is the complete Prepositional Phrase?
groups.plainExplanation: 'near the water tank' (Preposition 'near' + full Object 'the water tank').
groups.textbookRule: A Prepositional Phrase = Preposition + Noun / Noun Group / Object Pronoun (no finite verb).

structureSummary.patternNote: Prepositional Phrase = near (Preposition) + the water tank (Full Noun Group).

sentences.title: Compare Sentence · Object Pronoun Case
sentences.rawText: Mira shared ripe mangoes between Arjun and me.
sentences.note: After any preposition ('between, for, with, to'), always use Object-case pronouns ('me, us, him, her, them')—never 'between Arjun and I'!

tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Forces any following pronoun into Object case.
Part of the compound object after 'between'.

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'Mira' is the Subject.
groups.textbookRule: Pronouns after prepositions take Object case.

groups.label: Predicate
groups.plainExplanation: Because 'between' is a preposition, its object pronouns take Object case ('between Arjun and me').
groups.textbookRule: Always use Object-case pronouns (me, us, him, her, them, whom) after a preposition.

structureSummary.predicateText: shared ripe mangoes between Arjun and me.
structureSummary.patternNote: Preposition + Object Case: between (Preposition) + Arjun and me (Object Pronoun).

sentences.title: Starter Sentence · Time Scale (at / on / in)
sentences.rawText: Our assembly begins at eight on Mondays in July.
sentences.note: One clean scale: 'at' = exact clock point, 'on' = specific day/date, 'in' = longer month/season/year span!

tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Use 'at' for clock times, noon, midnight, and 'at night'.
Use 'on' for weekdays and calendar dates (on Monday, on 15 August).
Use 'in' for months, seasons, years, and 'in the morning/evening'.

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'Our assembly' is the Subject.
groups.textbookRule: Match 'at, on, in' to clock points, days/dates, and longer spans.

groups.label: Predicate (at + on + in)
groups.plainExplanation: 'at eight' (clock), 'on Mondays' (day), and 'in July' (month).
groups.textbookRule: Do NOT add at/on/in before 'yesterday, today, tomorrow, last/next week, every day'.

structureSummary.predicateText: begins at eight on Mondays in July.
structureSummary.patternNote: Time Scale: at (clock: eight) -> on (day: Mondays) -> in (month: July).

sentences.title: Starter Sentence · Start Point ('since') vs Length ('for')
sentences.rawText: Mira has practised music since June for one hour daily.
sentences.note: 'since' marks the starting point ('since June'), while 'for' measures total duration ('for one hour')!

tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Always followed by a point on the calendar/clock ('since June', 'since 2021').
Always followed by a measured length of time ('for one hour', 'for three years').

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'Mira' is the Subject.
groups.textbookRule: Use 'since' + starting point, and 'for' + total length of time.

groups.label: Predicate
groups.plainExplanation: 'since June' names when it began; 'for one hour' counts how long each session lasts.
groups.textbookRule: Use 'during' inside a named event ('during monsoon'), 'by' for a deadline, and 'until' for continuous duration up to a stop point.

structureSummary.predicateText: has practised music since June for one hour daily.
structureSummary.patternNote: since (Start Point: June) vs for (Length: one hour).

sentences.title: Compare Sentence · Deadline ('by') vs Endpoint ('until')
sentences.rawText: Return the library books by Friday; we stay open until four.
sentences.note: 'by Friday' = on or before Friday (deadline); 'until four' = open continuously up to 4:00 p.m.!

tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Use 'by' for a single-action deadline (submit by, finish by).
Use 'until/till' when an ongoing state stops at that time.

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'we' is the Subject of the second clause (understood 'you' in the first).
groups.textbookRule: Separate one-time deadlines ('by') from continuous states ('until').

groups.label: Predicate
groups.plainExplanation: Returning a book is a single act ('by Friday'); staying open continues up to a stop point ('until four').
groups.textbookRule: 'by' = not later than; 'until / till' = continuing up to.

structureSummary.predicateText: Return ... by Friday; stay open until four.
structureSummary.patternNote: by Friday (Deadline: on or before) vs until four (Continuous up to stop time).

sentences.title: Starter Sentence · Static Place (at / in / on)
sentences.rawText: Arjun waited at the gate while models sat in a box on the table.
sentences.note: Picture the space at rest: 'at' = specific point, 'in' = enclosed 3D space or city, 'on' = touching a flat surface!

tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Paired with meeting point 'at the gate'.
Use 'at' for spots, gates, bus stops, desks, and events.
Use 'in' for boxes, rooms, cities, and countries.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Resting on top of a flat surface.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Use 'on' for tables, walls, shelves, and floors.

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'Arjun' is the main Subject.
groups.textbookRule: Choose 'at, in, on' by how you picture the place: point, 3D interior, or surface.

groups.label: Predicate
groups.questionPrompt: How do 'at, in, on' picture space?
groups.plainExplanation: 'at the gate' (point), 'in a box' (inside), 'on the table' (on a surface).
groups.textbookRule: Walls and charts take 'on' ('a notice on the wall', not 'in the wall').

structureSummary.predicateText: waited at the gate while models sat in a box on the table.
structureSummary.patternNote: Static Place: at (point: gate) · in (enclosure: box) · on (surface: table).

sentences.title: Starter Sentence · Spatial Pairs (between / among)
sentences.rawText: The sapling stands between two trees among tall ferns.
sentences.note: Use 'between' for two distinct items, and 'among' inside a larger group of three or more!

tokens.meaningInSentence: Places the sapling with one tree on each side.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Used for two distinct items (or individually named items).
Used inside a group of three or more.

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'The sapling' is the Subject.
groups.textbookRule: Use 'between' for two items and 'among' inside a larger group.

groups.label: Predicate
groups.questionPrompt: Why 'between two trees' but 'among tall ferns'?
groups.plainExplanation: 'two trees' gives two landmarks ('between'); 'tall ferns' is a whole surrounding group ('among').
groups.textbookRule: Also separate 'beside' (next to) from 'besides' (in addition to), and 'in front of' from 'opposite' (facing across).

structureSummary.predicateText: stands between two trees among tall ferns.
structureSummary.patternNote: between (two distinct landmarks) vs among (surrounded by a group).

sentences.title: Starter Sentence · Entry Motion ('into')
sentences.rawText: Mira poured warm milk into the steel tumbler.
sentences.note: 'poured ... into' shows movement from outside to inside! Once it finishes moving, it rests 'in' the tumbler.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Moves liquid from jug to tumbler.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Action of moving inside calls for 'into'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Shows movement across the rim into the inside.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Use 'into' (not 'in') for entry motion from outside to inside.

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'Mira' is the Subject.
groups.textbookRule: Pair entry motion verbs with 'into' and surface-landing motion with 'onto'.

groups.label: Predicate
groups.plainExplanation: 'poured' describes motion from outside to inside, so English marks that crossing with 'into'.
groups.textbookRule: Separate destination reached ('to') from heading in a direction ('towards').

structureSummary.predicateText: poured warm milk into the steel tumbler.
structureSummary.patternNote: Motion Entry: poured (motion) + into the steel tumbler (outside -> inside).

sentences.title: Compare Sentence · Static Rest ('in')
sentences.rawText: Now the warm milk is in the steel tumbler.
sentences.note: No movement now—just resting inside! So static location uses 'in', not 'into'.

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'the warm milk' is the Subject.
groups.textbookRule: Use 'in' and 'on' for rest; 'into' and 'onto' for movement.

groups.label: Predicate
groups.plainExplanation: 'is' expresses a quiet state of rest inside, so 'in' (not 'into') fits.
groups.textbookRule: Motion verbs take 'into'; resting states take 'in'.

structureSummary.predicateText: is in the steel tumbler now.
structureSummary.patternNote: Static Rest: is (rest) + in the steel tumbler (already inside).

sentences.title: Starter Sentence · Path Shapes (across / through)
sentences.rawText: The cyclists rode across the bridge and through the forest.
sentences.note: Picture the shape: 'across' crosses a flat surface from side to side; 'through' enters and passes inside a 3D space!

tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Verb describing travel along a route.

tokens.meaningInSentence: From one side to the other over a surface.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Use 'across' for bridges, roads, fields, and rivers.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Enters, moves inside, and exits a 3D space.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Use 'through' for tunnels, forests, crowds, and open windows.

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'The cyclists' is the Subject.
groups.textbookRule: Match path prepositions to geometry: surface ('across'), 3D tunnel/trees ('through'), or line ('along').

groups.label: Predicate
groups.plainExplanation: 'across the bridge' goes over an open surface; 'through the forest' goes inside surrounded by trees.
groups.textbookRule: Use 'along' when following the length of a road, canal, or river bank.

structureSummary.predicateText: rode across the bridge and through the forest.
structureSummary.patternNote: Paths: across (2D surface: bridge) · through (3D volume: forest).

sentences.title: Compare Sentence · Linear Path ('along')
sentences.rawText: Evening walkers strolled slowly along the river bank.
sentences.note: Instead of crossing side-to-side ('across'), 'along' follows the length of a line or edge!

tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Use 'along' for paths, corridors, canals, and river banks.

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'Evening walkers' is the Subject.
groups.textbookRule: 'along' follows a line; 'across' goes from one side to the other.

groups.label: Predicate
groups.plainExplanation: Walkers stay on the bank following its length ('along the river bank'), not crossing over water ('across').
groups.textbookRule: Pair linear paths (corridors, roads, shores) with 'along'.

structureSummary.predicateText: strolled slowly along the river bank.
structureSummary.patternNote: Linear Path: along the river bank (following the line lengthwise).

sentences.title: Starter Sentence · Tool ('with') & Means ('by')
sentences.rawText: Arjun sliced fresh papaya with a knife and rode home by bus.
sentences.note: Use 'with' for physical tools ('with a knife'), 'by + vehicle' (no 'a/the') for travel—except 'on foot' and 'in a car'!

tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Paired with tool phrase 'with a knife'.
Always 'with' (never 'by') before a tool like 'a knife'.
Use 'by + vehicle' with NO article ('by bus, by train'), and 'on foot' for walking.

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'Arjun' is the Subject.
groups.textbookRule: Distinguish tool ('with'), transport ('by' vs 'on foot'), and material ('made of / from').

groups.label: Predicate
groups.questionPrompt: Which prepositions show tool and travel?
groups.plainExplanation: 'with a knife' (tool) and 'by bus' (transport mode; walking is always 'on foot').
groups.textbookRule: Use 'by' for vehicle mode without 'a/the' ('by train'), 'in a car', and 'on foot'.

structureSummary.predicateText: sliced fresh papaya with a knife and rode home by bus.
structureSummary.patternNote: with (Tool: a knife) · by (Transport: bus; walking = on foot).

sentences.title: Compare Sentence · Material ('made of' vs 'made from')
sentences.rawText: School benches are made of wood while curd is made from milk.
sentences.note: If you can still see the original material -> 'made of' (wood). If it transforms into something new -> 'made from' (milk -> curd)!

tokens.meaningInSentence: Wood stays visible inside the bench.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Use 'made of' when physical material stays recognisable.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Milk changes form completely into curd.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Use 'made from' when original substance changes form/nature.

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'School benches' is the Subject.
groups.textbookRule: Use 'made of' for unchanged visible materials and 'made from' for transformed ingredients.

groups.label: Predicate
groups.plainExplanation: Wood still looks like wood in a bench ('made of'); milk ferments into curd ('made from').
groups.textbookRule: Physical preservation -> 'of'; transformation -> 'from'.

structureSummary.predicateText: are made of wood while curd is made from milk.
structureSummary.patternNote: made of (visible: wood) vs made from (transformed: milk -> curd).

sentences.title: Starter Sentence · One Preposition, Shifting Contexts
sentences.rawText: By noon we reached the garden by the river by bicycle.
sentences.note: Watch 'by' change jobs three times in one sentence: Time ('by noon'), Place ('by the river'), and Transport ('by bicycle')!

tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Same word 'by', here expressing Time deadline.

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'we' is the Subject.
groups.textbookRule: Prepositions do not have one rigid meaning—always read the surrounding context.

groups.label: Predicate (3 Roles of 'by')
groups.questionPrompt: How does 'by' change across the sentence?
groups.plainExplanation: 1) 'By noon' (Time deadline), 2) 'by the river' (Place beside), 3) 'by bicycle' (Transport means).
groups.textbookRule: Context also determines whether 'in' means place ('in the box'), time ('in July'), medium ('in ink'), or state ('in a hurry').

structureSummary.predicateText: reached the garden by the river by bicycle by noon.
structureSummary.patternNote: Context Chameleon: By noon (Time) · by the river (Place) · by bicycle (Means).

sentences.title: Starter Sentence · Zero-Preposition Verbs & 'within'
sentences.rawText: Our team discussed the rainwater plan and reached the hall within ten minutes.
sentences.note: Do NOT write 'discussed about' or 'reached to/at'! And 'within ten minutes' means before 10 minutes pass.

tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Transitive verb taking 'the rainwater plan' directly.
Contrast: 'within' = anytime before the end; 'in' = at the end of.

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'Our team' is the Subject.
groups.textbookRule: Transitive verbs like 'discuss, enter, reach, order, await, resemble' take Direct Objects without prepositions.

groups.label: Predicate
groups.plainExplanation: 'discussed the rainwater plan' (no 'about') and 'reached the hall' (no 'to/at').
groups.textbookRule: Use 'within' for 'before the end of a period' vs 'in' for 'at the end of'.

structureSummary.predicateText: discussed the rainwater plan and reached the hall within ten minutes.
structureSummary.patternNote: Zero-Prep Verbs: discussed + plan | reached + hall (not 'about/to').

sentences.title: Compare Sentence · Natural Question Placement
sentences.rawText: Which laboratory shelf did Mira leave the microscope on?
sentences.note: Even though prepositions usually precede their objects, ending a Wh-question with 'on?' is completely natural English!

tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Moved to the front to form the Wh-question.
Natural end-placed preposition in Wh-questions (never drop 'on'!).

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'Mira' is the Subject.
groups.textbookRule: Prepositions normally precede their objects, but move naturally to the end in Wh-questions and relative clauses.

groups.label: Predicate
groups.plainExplanation: Its object ('Which laboratory shelf') moved to the front of the question, leaving 'on?' cleanly at the end.
groups.textbookRule: Do not omit the preposition at the end of a question like 'What are you writing with?'

structureSummary.predicateText: Which laboratory shelf did ... leave the microscope on?

teachingSequence.title: What Prepositions Do: Relation Bridges
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: A preposition bridges a noun or pronoun to the rest of the sentence—swapping one preposition changes the whole scene!
teachingSequence.explanation: Prepositions show how things relate in space, time, direction, or means. Compare 'on the wooden bench' with 'under the wooden bench' using the Compare Sentence tab.

clausePatternData.whyItWorks: Without 'on', 'sits' and 'the wooden bench' cannot connect cleanly. The preposition acts as a directional bridge between the action ('sits') and the landmark ('the wooden bench').
clausePatternData.ruleSummary: A preposition links a noun or pronoun to another word; changing the preposition changes the relationship and meaning.

keyTerms.meaning: A small bridge word ('on, under, in, near, by, with') placed before a noun/pronoun to show relation.
The noun, noun group, or object pronoun that completes the preposition ('the wooden bench').

relationDiagram.caption: Changing only the bridge word moves the bottle from top to underneath to next to the bench.

progressiveExamples.sentence: The mango sits on / under / beside the wooden table.
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) Keep 'mango' and 'table' identical. 2) Swap 'on' (top) -> 'under' (below) -> 'beside' (next to).
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Every swap paints a new real-world picture.

progressiveExamples.sentence: Mira waited for / with / near Arjun.
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) 'waited for Arjun' = expecting him. 2) 'waited with Arjun' = waiting together. 3) 'waited near Arjun' = distance.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Prepositions control abstract social meanings too, not just space.

progressiveExamples.sentence: The wooden basket of ripe guavas sat behind the kitchen door.
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) 'of ripe guavas' attaches to noun 'basket'. 2) 'behind the kitchen door' tells where it 'sat'.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Prepositional phrases can describe nouns OR verbs.

commonMistake.incorrectText: Treating prepositions as meaningless filler words that can be guessed randomly.
commonMistake.correctText: Picture the exact relation ('on' vs 'under', 'for' vs 'with') before choosing.
commonMistake.whyWrong: Changing one tiny preposition reverses or breaks the sentence's meaning.

teachingSequence.title: Prepositional Phrases, Object Pronouns & Clause Test
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Always group [Preposition + full Noun Group / Object Pronoun] into one Prepositional Phrase—and test words like 'before / after' to see if a clause follows!
teachingSequence.explanation: A Prepositional Phrase never has a finite verb. When a pronoun follows a preposition, use Object case ('between Arjun and me'). And if a finite verb follows 'before/after', it acts as a clause linker instead!

clausePatternData.whyItWorks: Determiners and adjectives inside a noun group ('the school water tank') belong strictly inside the Prepositional Phrase. After any preposition, pronouns take Object case ('me, us, him, her, them').
clausePatternData.ruleSummary: Group Preposition + full Noun Group or Object Pronoun ('between you and me'); Preposition + Noun != Conjunction + Clause.

progressiveExamples.sentence: She placed the clay pot under the cool neem tree.
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) Preposition: 'under'. 2) Full noun-group object: 'the cool neem tree'.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: The complete phrase is 'under the cool neem tree'—never stop at 'under' alone.

progressiveExamples.sentence: The coach divided the oranges between Priya and him.
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) Spot preposition 'between'. 2) Choose Object case 'him' (never 'he').
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Every pronoun after a preposition sits in the Object slot.

progressiveExamples.sentence: After morning assembly (Preposition) vs After morning assembly ended (Conjunction).
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) 'after morning assembly' -> noun phrase only (no finite verb) = Preposition. 2) 'ended' = finite verb -> Conjunction!
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Works for before, after, since, and until.

commonMistake.incorrectText: Please keep this secret between you and I.
commonMistake.correctText: Please keep this secret between you and me.
commonMistake.whyWrong: 'between' is a preposition, so both pronouns are its objects -> 'you and me'.

boardNote.label: Grammar Note · Prepositional Phrases Have No Finite Verb
boardNote.text: An '-ing' verbal noun can also follow a preposition ('by reading carefully', 'before leaving'), but a Prepositional Phrase itself never contains a finite verb.

checkpointData.prompt: In 'Fresh spinach grows well near the school water tank', which group of words is the complete Prepositional Phrase?

options.label: near
options.explanation: The preposition alone is incomplete without its object.

options.label: grows well near
options.explanation: A Prepositional Phrase never grabs the verb ('grows').

options.label: near the school water tank
options.explanation: Begins with preposition 'near' and ends at the end of its noun-group object 'the school water tank'.

teachingSequence.title: Prepositions of Time: 'at', 'on', 'in' & Zero-Preposition Words
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Match time prepositions to size: 'at' (clock point), 'on' (day/date), 'in' (month/season/year)—and NEVER add them before yesterday, today, tomorrow, or next/last + day!
teachingSequence.explanation: Instead of memorising random phrases, picture time as zooming out: exact point ('at 8 a.m.'), single calendar day ('on Monday'), or broad span ('in July').

clausePatternData.categoryBadge: Topic 2 · The Time Scale + Zero Trap
clausePatternData.whyItWorks: English scales time like geometry: a 0D point takes 'at' (at noon, at night), a 1-day surface takes 'on' (on 15 August), and a 3D container span takes 'in' (in July, in 2024, in the morning).
clausePatternData.ruleSummary: at = clock points & night; on = days & dates; in = months, seasons, years & morning/evening; NONE before yesterday/today/tomorrow/next/last.

segments.label: AT · Point
segments.text: at eight, at noon, at night

segments.label: IN · Longer Span
segments.text: in July, in 2024, in the morning

progressiveExamples.sentence: We eat a healthy breakfast at 7:30 a.m. in the morning.
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) Clock time '7:30 a.m.' -> 'at'. 2) Span 'the morning' -> 'in' (note exception: 'at night').
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Watch 'in the morning/evening' vs 'at night'.

progressiveExamples.sentence: India celebrates Independence Day on 15 August.
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) Even though 'August' alone takes 'in August', adding day number '15' makes it a specific date -> 'on 15 August'.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Any specific day or date takes 'on' (even 'on Friday morning').

progressiveExamples.sentence: The eco-club will plant saplings next Saturday (NOT 'on next Saturday').
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) Spot 'next', 'last', 'this', 'every', 'yesterday', 'today', or 'tomorrow'. 2) Leave out 'on / in / at' completely.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Time adverbs with this/next/last/every replace the preposition.

commonMistake.incorrectText: We will meet for garden duty on tomorrow in Monday.
commonMistake.correctText: We will meet for garden duty tomorrow on Monday.
commonMistake.whyWrong: 'tomorrow' takes NO preposition, and days of the week take 'on' (never 'in Monday').

teachingSequence.title: Duration & Time Limits: 'since', 'for', 'during', 'by' & 'until'
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Use 'since' for starting points, 'for' for total length, 'during' inside a named event, 'by' for deadlines, and 'until' for continuous endpoints.
teachingSequence.explanation: Even when two sentences talk about time, a starting point ('since 2021') needs a different bridge from a length ('for three years')—and a one-shot deadline ('by Friday') differs from staying open ('until four').

clausePatternData.whyItWorks: 'since' pins the start date on the timeline (2021 -> now); 'for' measures the bar's length (3 years). Meanwhile, 'by' sets a finish line for a single action, whereas 'until' stretches an ongoing state up to a stop point.
clausePatternData.ruleSummary: since + start point | for + duration | during + named event | by + deadline | until + continuous stop point.

progressiveExamples.sentence: The eco-club has watered the orchard for five years, since 2021.
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) 'five years' = how long (duration) -> 'for'. 2) '2021' = starting point -> 'since'.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Never write 'since five years' or 'for 2021'.

progressiveExamples.sentence: Students read astronomy charts during the winter camp.
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) 'the winter camp' is a named period/event (not a number of hours). 2) Use 'during' (not 'for the winter camp' if telling when).
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: 'during' answers 'when/inside what event?'; 'for' answers 'how long?'

progressiveExamples.sentence: Finish your science poster by Thursday; the art room stays open until 5 p.m.
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) Finishing the poster happens by a deadline -> 'by Thursday'. 2) Staying open continues -> 'until 5 p.m.'.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: 'Return the book until Friday' is wrong because returning happens once, not continuously.

commonMistake.incorrectText: The eco-club has planted saplings since three years; return tools until Friday.
commonMistake.correctText: The eco-club has planted saplings for three years; return tools by Friday.
commonMistake.whyWrong: 'three years' is a length ('for'), and returning tools is a deadline ('by').

checkpointData.prompt: Choose the accurate completion: 'Mira has practised classical music ___ 2021, and she practises ___ an hour every evening.'

options.label: for ... since
options.explanation: '2021' is a starting point, not a count of years.

options.label: since ... for
options.explanation: '2021' is the starting point ('since 2021'), whereas 'an hour' measures duration ('for an hour').

options.label: by ... until
options.explanation: 'by 2021' and 'until an hour' do not express start point and duration.

teachingSequence.title: Static Place: Point ('at'), Enclosure ('in') & Surface ('on')
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: For places at rest, picture the space: 'at' = specific point or stop, 'in' = inside a box, room, or city, 'on' = touching a flat surface.
teachingSequence.explanation: Once you picture how a speaker views a place—as a map dot ('at'), an enclosed 3D space ('in'), or a flat surface ('on')—choosing place prepositions becomes visual and clear.

clausePatternData.whyItWorks: In 'at the gate', the gate is a pinpoint meeting spot. In 'in a box', the models are enclosed inside walls. In 'on the table', the box rests directly on the flat top surface.
clausePatternData.ruleSummary: at = point or address; in = enclosed container, room, city, or country; on = touching a surface or line.

keyTerms.meaning: Pinpoints a spot, meeting place, or address: at the school gate, at the bus stop, at desk 4.
Inside boundaries: in the tiffin box, in the library, in Jaipur, in Kerala, in India.
Touching a surface or street/bank: on the table, on the chalkboard, on the wall, on the first floor.

progressiveExamples.sentence: Fresh sprouts are packed in the clean tiffin box on the kitchen shelf.
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) Inside a container -> 'in the clean tiffin box'. 2) Resting on a shelf surface -> 'on the kitchen shelf'.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Distinguishes interior from surface.

progressiveExamples.sentence: Wait at the bus stop; our friends live in Guwahati.
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) A bus stop along a route is a meeting point -> 'at'. 2) A whole city encloses streets -> 'in'.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Matches scale cleanly.

progressiveExamples.sentence: Compare: 'A student sits at a desk' (position near) vs 'The notebook lies on the desk' (surface) vs 'A pen is in the desk drawer' (inside).
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) Sitting to study = 'at'. 2) Touching desktop = 'on'. 3) Inside drawer = 'in'.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Shows why you choose by relation, not by noun!

commonMistake.incorrectText: The science poster was pinned in the classroom wall.
commonMistake.correctText: The science poster was pinned on the classroom wall.
commonMistake.whyWrong: A wall is a flat surface, so notices and posters sit 'on' the wall—not buried inside it.

teachingSequence.title: Spatial Pairs: between / among, beside / besides & opposite
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Keep high-confusion pairs sharp: 'between' (two) vs 'among' (group), 'beside' (next to) vs 'besides' (in addition to), and 'in front of' vs 'opposite'.
teachingSequence.explanation: A single letter ('beside' vs 'besides') or group size ('between' vs 'among') completely shifts meaning when describing people and landmarks.

clausePatternData.whyItWorks: 'between' marks a space separating two clear items (or individually named partners), while 'among' surrounds something inside a crowd of three or more. Meanwhile, 'beside' is spatial ('next to'), while 'besides' adds another item ('apart from').
clausePatternData.ruleSummary: between = two (or named items); among = group of 3+; beside = next to; besides = in addition to; opposite = facing across.

segments.label: beside vs besides
segments.subLabel: Do not add extra -s for place

progressiveExamples.sentence: Mira sat beside Arjun during the science quiz.
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) 'next to' -> 'beside' (without -s). 2) Reserve 'besides' for 'Besides Arjun, two girls also presented charts.'
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Removes the common extra '-s' error.

progressiveExamples.sentence: The library sits opposite the main playground (across facing it), right in front of the mango grove.
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) 'opposite' = across a courtyard/road facing each other. 2) 'in front of' = ahead in the same line/order.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Separates facing across from lining ahead.

progressiveExamples.sentence: Notice: 'over' often implies directly covering ('a roof over our heads'), while 'above' simply means higher on a scale/level ('above sea level').
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) Vertical cover -> 'over' / 'under' ('under the shade of the tree'). 2) Higher/lower level -> 'above' / 'below' ('below zero').
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Matches both physical shelter and measurement scales.

commonMistake.incorrectText: The coach divided the fresh oranges between all twenty players; Mira sat besides Arjun.
commonMistake.correctText: The coach divided the fresh oranges among all twenty players; Mira sat beside Arjun.
commonMistake.whyWrong: 'twenty players' is a group ('among'), and 'next to' is 'beside' (without -s).

options.label: The coach divided the fresh oranges between all twenty players.
options.explanation: A group of twenty players requires 'among', not 'between'.

options.label: Mira sat besides Arjun during the astronomy quiz.
The library sits between the science laboratory and the art room.
options.explanation: 'between' accurately links two distinct named locations.

teachingSequence.title: Direction & Motion: Static ('in / on') vs Entry ('into / onto') & 'to / towards'
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Separate resting inside/on ('in, on') from moving from outside to inside/top ('into, onto'), and goal reached ('to') from heading in that direction ('towards').
teachingSequence.explanation: Compare 'poured warm milk into the tumbler' (entry motion) with 'milk is in the tumbler' (quiet rest) using the Compare Sentence tab!

clausePatternData.whyItWorks: Action verbs like 'pour, walk, jump, step' cross a boundary from outside to inside ('into') or onto a surface ('onto'). Static verbs like 'is, sits, rests' stay inside ('in') or on top ('on').
clausePatternData.ruleSummary: Use into / onto for movement across a boundary; use in / on for resting location; use to (goal) vs towards (direction).

relationDiagram.caption: Motion verbs cross the boundary ('into'); resting states stay inside ('in').

progressiveExamples.sentence: The frog jumped into the pond (entry) and now swims in the pond (inside).
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) Jumping from bank to water crosses the boundary -> 'into'. 2) Swimming already inside the water -> 'in'.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Clearly separates crossing from staying inside.

progressiveExamples.sentence: The cat climbed onto the garden wall, and now sleeps on the wall.
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) Climbing up onto a surface -> 'onto'. 2) Sleeping already at rest there -> 'on'.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: 'onto' marks the landing movement.

progressiveExamples.sentence: We cycled to the museum (reached it), while monsoon clouds drifted towards the hills (heading in that direction).
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) 'to' signals reaching the destination. 2) 'towards' signals direction without claiming arrival.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Even 'from ... to' marks start origin to final endpoint.

commonMistake.incorrectText: Mira poured warm milk in the glass and walked in the hall.
commonMistake.correctText: Mira poured warm milk into the glass and walked into the hall.
commonMistake.whyWrong: Both pouring and walking from outside to inside express entry motion, so they take 'into'.

teachingSequence.title: Path Shapes: 'across', 'through' & 'along'
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Picture the shape of the path: 'across' crosses an open 2D surface, 'through' moves inside a 3D space or opening, and 'along' follows a line!
teachingSequence.explanation: Don't mix up 'across' and 'through'—a bridge goes across a river surface, whereas a tunnel or forest wraps around you on all sides ('through')!

clausePatternData.whyItWorks: 'across' travels from edge A to edge B over an open surface (bridge, playground, road). 'through' enters, passes inside, and exits a surrounded 3D volume (tunnel, forest, doorway). 'along' follows a narrow line or bank.
clausePatternData.ruleSummary: across = side-to-side over a 2D surface; through = inside a 3D volume or opening; along = following a line/edge.

progressiveExamples.sentence: Cool monsoon breeze entered through the open window.
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) Air passes inside a framed opening from outside to inside. 2) Use 'through' (never 'across the window').
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Openings and frames take 'through'.

progressiveExamples.sentence: Arjun walked across the playground to hand Mira the whistle.
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) A playground is an open flat surface from one side to the other. 2) Use 'across'.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: No surrounding tunnel/trees.

progressiveExamples.sentence: Cyclists rode along the canal path, across the stone bridge, and through the pine grove.
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) Edge of canal = 'along'. 2) Crossing bridge surface = 'across'. 3) Inside trees = 'through'.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Each preposition matches its physical path.

commonMistake.incorrectText: The train sped across the dark mountain tunnel.
commonMistake.correctText: The train sped through the dark mountain tunnel.
commonMistake.whyWrong: A tunnel encloses the train on top and both sides (3D volume), so it requires 'through', not 'across'.

checkpointData.prompt: Fill the blanks accurately: 'The train passed ___ a long tunnel and then crossed a bridge ___ the Godavari River.'

options.label: across ... through
options.explanation: A tunnel is enclosed in 3D ('through'), and a bridge spans a surface ('across').

options.label: through ... across
options.explanation: Trains move inside a tunnel ('through') and over a bridge from bank to bank ('across').

options.label: along ... into
options.explanation: 'along a tunnel' and 'into the river' distort the train's route.

teachingSequence.title: Tools ('with'), Transport ('by / on foot') & Material ('of / from')
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Use 'with' for physical tools, 'by + vehicle' (no 'a/the') for travel—except 'on foot' and 'in a car'—and 'made of' (visible) vs 'made from' (transformed).
teachingSequence.explanation: Prepositions don't just mark time and space! They also show what tool you held, how you travelled, and whether an ingredient changed form.

clausePatternData.whyItWorks: 'with' connects a hand-held tool ('with a knife'), while 'by' connects a general mode of travel ('by bus, by train') or human doer ('by Arjun'). For materials, 'of' keeps raw form visible ('of wood'), while 'from' signals transformation ('from milk').
clausePatternData.ruleSummary: Tool = with; Vehicle mode (no article) = by (but walking = on foot, private car = in a car); Material = made of (visible) vs made from (changed).

segments.label: TRAVEL · BY / ON
segments.text: by bus / in a car / on foot

progressiveExamples.sentence: Most students come to our village school on foot, while others arrive by bicycle.
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) Walking is ALWAYS 'on foot' (never 'by foot'). 2) Vehicle without 'a/the' -> 'by bicycle / by bus'.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Fixes one of the most frequent travel slips.

progressiveExamples.sentence: Write your lab observations in blue ink with a neat pen.
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) Liquid/colour medium -> 'in blue ink' (or 'in pencil'). 2) Physical object held -> 'with a pen'.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Separates writing medium from writing instrument.

progressiveExamples.sentence: Clay pots are made of clay (still clay), whereas fresh cheese is made from warm milk (changed substance).
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) You still see and touch clay -> 'made of'. 2) Milk transforms completely -> 'made from'.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Clear visual test for material prepositions.

commonMistake.incorrectText: Arjun sliced the papaya by a knife and walked to school by foot.
commonMistake.correctText: Arjun sliced the papaya with a knife and walked to school on foot.
commonMistake.whyWrong: Instruments take 'with' (not 'by'), and walking always takes 'on foot' (not 'by foot').

checkpointData.prompt: Which sentence uses means, tool, or material prepositions accurately?

options.label: She tightened the telescope screw by a small screwdriver.
options.explanation: A screwdriver is a tool -> use 'with a small screwdriver'.

options.label: Butter is churned from fresh cream, and many pupils walk to school on foot.
options.explanation: 'from' marks transformed origin (cream -> butter), and walking is always 'on foot'.

options.label: Mira came to the library in bus this morning.
options.explanation: Use 'by bus' (no article) or 'on a bus' (with article).

teachingSequence.title: Context Chameleons: How One Preposition Shifts Meaning
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Never memorise one single meaning for a preposition! Context decides whether 'by' or 'in' marks Place, Time, Means, Medium, or State.
teachingSequence.explanation: Watch one sentence use 'by' three ways: 'By noon' (Time), 'by the river' (Place), and 'by bicycle' (Means). Always read the words beside the preposition!

clausePatternData.whyItWorks: The word 'by' has no single fixed meaning on its own. Paired with a clock time ('noon'), it marks a deadline; paired with a landmark ('the river'), it means beside; paired with a vehicle ('bicycle'), it marks transport; paired with an author ('Tagore'), it marks the creator.
clausePatternData.ruleSummary: Do not assign one rigid rule per preposition; check context (Time, Place, Means, Medium, Doer, or State).

progressiveExamples.sentence: 'in' shifts too: in the box (Place) · in July (Time) · in blue ink (Medium) · in a hurry (State).
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) Box = space inside. 2) July = time span. 3) Blue ink = writing medium. 4) A hurry = state/manner.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Every meaning follows cleanly from the object noun.

progressiveExamples.sentence: Compare verb + preposition pairs: care for saplings · look at the chart · wait for the train · listen to the guide.
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) Look + 'at' (focus gaze) vs Look + 'for' (search). 2) Listen ALWAYS pairs with 'to' before what you hear.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Meaning lives in the partnership between verb and preposition.

progressiveExamples.sentence: Compare 'agree with a person/idea' vs 'agree to a plan/proposal' vs 'agree on a date'.
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) Person/opinion -> 'agree with Mira'. 2) Proposal/terms -> 'agree to the plan'. 3) Shared decision -> 'agree on Monday'.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Choosing by context prevents common exam mistakes.

commonMistake.incorrectText: Assuming 'by' only belongs in Passive Voice or 'in' only means physical inside-ness.
commonMistake.correctText: Read the noun after the preposition to identify Time, Place, Means, Medium, or State.
commonMistake.whyWrong: High-frequency prepositions carry multiple contextual meanings across everyday English.

teachingSequence.title: Zero-Preposition Verbs, 'in / within', Placement & Phrasal Boundary
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Drop extra prepositions after 'discuss, enter, reach, order, resemble'; split 'in' (at end) vs 'within' (before end); and keep question-end prepositions natural!
teachingSequence.explanation: Finish strong by clearing four classic exam and everyday traps—including knowing when a word like 'up' is a real Preposition vs part of an idiomatic Phrasal Verb.

clausePatternData.whyItWorks: Verbs like 'discuss' (= talk about), 'enter' (= go into), and 'reach' (= arrive at) already carry the relation inside the verb itself—so adding 'about / into / to' repeats it twice! Meanwhile, in Wh-questions ('Which shelf did Mira leave it on?'), moving the object to the front naturally strands 'on?' at the end.
clausePatternData.ruleSummary: Never add about/into/to after discuss, enter, reach, order; 'within' = before period ends; ending a Wh-question with a preposition is natural.

segments.label: Zero-Prep Verbs
segments.text: discussed the plan / reached the hall

segments.label: Phrasal Boundary
segments.text: look up chimney vs look up word

progressiveExamples.sentence: The students entered the hall quietly (NOT 'entered into the hall') and ordered fresh fruit.
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) 'enter' + physical room takes NO 'into' (save 'enter into' for abstract agreements/contracts). 2) 'order' takes NO 'for'.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Contrast with 'arrive at/in' and 'listen to', which DO need prepositions.

progressiveExamples.sentence: The parcel arrives within two days (anytime before 2 days end) vs in two days (at the 2-day mark).
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) Upper limit before deadline expires -> 'within'. 2) Exact period until completion -> 'in'.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Gives precision in schedules and promises.

progressiveExamples.sentence: Look up the chimney (Preposition + noun) vs Look up a word in a dictionary (Phrasal Verb = search).
progressiveExamples.stepByStep: 1) 'up the chimney' keeps literal upward direction. 2) 'look up' meaning 'search' is a single idiomatic Phrasal Verb.
progressiveExamples.whyCorrect: Keeps Prepositions cleanly separated from Phrasal Verbs.

commonMistake.incorrectText: Our team discussed about the rainwater project and reached to the hall.
commonMistake.correctText: Our team discussed the rainwater project and reached the hall.
commonMistake.whyWrong: 'discuss' and 'reach' are transitive verbs that connect directly to their objects without 'about' or 'to'.

boardNote.label: Grammar Note · Formal vs Everyday Question Placement
boardNote.text: Everyday English naturally places the preposition at the end of a question ('What are you writing with?'). Formal writing sometimes fronts it before 'whom/which' ('With what are you writing?' / 'The shelf on which...').

checkpointData.prompt: Which sentence is completely free of preposition errors?

options.label: Our team discussed about the rainwater project after lunch.
Arjun reached at the railway station ten minutes early.
options.explanation: 'reach' takes a direct object without 'at/to' (compare 'arrived at').

options.label: Which laboratory shelf did Mira leave the microscope on?
options.explanation: Question-end placement ('leave the microscope on?') is natural English and keeps the required preposition!
